activity.title: This past week I was locked in at LinkedIn HQ in Sunnyvale for the Possibilities in Tech hackathon. Glad to share two updates. First, I’m honored to have been selected as a winner of Apple ’s Swift Student Challenge, out of thousands of applicants worldwide. For my submission, I built Lenzo — an app that uses CoreML, Foundational Models, and subject lifting to help people learn languages in real time, anytime, anywhere. The goal was to make language learning feel seamless and integrated into everyday life. Second, I’m thrilled to share that I’ll be joining Amazon this summer as a Software Engineering Intern in Seattle, WA. Grateful for these opportunities and excited for what’s ahead.

Humbled. With God’s grace, I’m humbled to share that last week I wrapped up my 12-week Software Engineering and Product Management Explorer internship with Microsoft , under M365 Core. This summer, together with my podmates, I architected and implemented an agentic AI solution that enabled internal service engineers to onboard and simulate realistic test traffic for their services, reducing onboarding time from 3 weeks to under 15 minutes. Words can’t express how grateful I am for this opportunity and how transformative it was. I will surely remember the project (in Chisom ’s words), but the people are the ones I’ll truly miss the most. Thank you to my manager, Isaac, my mentors Lina and Vaishnavee , and especially Sebastián , who truly believed in me and my awesome podmates, Kamsi and Nazifa . You saw the potential in us and pushed us to grow. We couldn’t have wished for a better team. Also, thank you to Shanon , Kristin , and Jane for making the program so memorable and truly one of the best experiences of my life. And to everyone I met here, you all had a mark on my growth as a software engineer and as a person. I was truly lucky to meet and work alongside some of the smartest and most talented minds on earth.

Excited to announce that my team and I took 2nd place at the Amazon Intern Hackathon! Early in the summer I got blocked on my own project for a while. Different root cause, but the feeling stuck with me: knowing exactly what you want to build and losing days to figuring out who can unblock you. Then I started hearing the same thing from interns across completely different orgs. Who owns this package. Why can't I access this. Everyone had a workaround, nobody had an answer, and every one of them assumed it was just their team's quirk. It wasn't. When the same friction shows up independently across that many teams, it stops being a people problem and becomes a systems problem. That's the kind worth building for. So when the theme came out as "Pay It Forward," we already knew what we were solving. We built Path. Under the hood, it's a knowledge map of who owns what, who can approve what, and how code actually moves to prod. You type a question the way you'd ask a coworker, and instead of a search results page you get a short list of names, ranked by who can actually unblock you, each one linked to their profile. The answer is a person, not a doc. The hard part wasn't building the map. It was cutting everything that wasn't the map. We scrapped features the night before demos and the product got sharper every time. Shoutout to my teammates Andrew Lin , Ava Martoma , and Jacob Ryabinky . I've never seen a team disagree that productively at 1 am. Huge thanks to Emma Hanan , Betty Beniam , and the rest of the AFE team who put this amazing event together!

Thrilled to share that my team and I just took 2nd place at the Amazon AFE Hackathon! Working internally at Amazon this summer has given me a firsthand look at how massive the organizational structure can be, especially for a new employee. Inspired by this year's theme of "Pay It Forward," we built Path, an evidence-backed knowledge graph designed to help new engineers and interns "find their path from Day One." Ask a normal question in plain English -- "Who owns this package?" or "Can I edit this in prod?" -- and Path traces the real ownership, access, and deployment paths across teams, packages, pipelines, and accounts. It then returns a ranked list of exactly who to reach out to, with a link straight to their internal Amazon profile. A huge thank you to my incredible teammates Daniel Lee , Jacob Ryabinky , and Andrew Lin for the amazing teamwork. Thank you also to Betty Beniam , Emma Hanan , and everyone who helped make the hackathon happen. Looking forward to more great work! #Amazon #Hackathon #PayItForward #Innovation

Great conversation this week with our 2026 Amazon interns about what AI means for their careers. Here's a piece of advice I shared with them. When I started out, a new person coming into a job could only have so much impact in their first year. That's changed. If you learn from the beginning how to work with AI as a force multiplier, you can accomplish more, move faster, and take on real responsibility much sooner than you otherwise would. This class is already working that way. They're AI native in a way that makes the teams they join better. Thanks to Anika Suman , an SDE intern on AWS Deadline Cloud, for moderating. To all our interns: thank you for choosing Amazon.

I am very grateful to have had the opportunity to attend the Datadog x ColorStack IRL event at Datadog's NYC office. It was an incredible experience getting to hear directly from engineers and current interns about their work, career journeys, and what it's like to be part of the company. As I wrap up my summer as an Engineering Intern at Swagelok , I want to take a moment to reflect on an incredible experience. Coming into my first engineering internship, I was excited to learn and grow while seeing how my project scope sheets turn into fully implemented systems on the manufacturing floor. These last several months have done all of that and more. I had the opportunity to work on projects that challenged me technically, developed my leadership and communication skills, and gave me a new point of view on manufacturing operations. From my first day doing orientation at the Distribution Center, to the Summer in The Land Guardians game, to being the captain of the winning Cleveland Corporate Challenge Arcade Basketball team, to giving my final presentation. Every moment here has been an opportunity for me to succeed, and I couldn't appreciate it more. My supervisors Trent Babcock and Dean Peska have been nothing but supportive throughout the entire summer and with their guidance I've been able to work on meaningful projects that allowed me to take ownership for projects I never would've imagined receiving as an intern. For my first project, huge thanks to my project sponsor Micheal Zickes for working with me on this, I was given a project focused on digitizing production reports. I developed VBA macros for production documentation with integrated barcode scanning, improved validation logic, and PDF generation to improve efficiency, data security, and customer ease of use. I was able to work with operators to refine this form to their liking and decrease the time taken to complete these forms from when it was completed manually by around 80% (roughly 2 minutes 30 seconds to roughly 30 seconds) with a decrease in errors in the form to 0% because of the increased data security. For my second project, another massive thank you to my technical sponsor Micheal Duplay for all of your assistance, I was assigned to support updates on a vision system workstation. For this project, I was able to learn how to use Studio 5000 and FactoryTalk View to update code with new instructions on a process logic controller (PLC) and new images on a human machine interface (HMI) to help make part assembly more efficient. This gave me a massive insight into the future of manufacturing and what controls engineers do on a daily basis. The team and I were successfully able to get the vision system updated and it is now up and running at an improved capacity! Beyond the technical work, one of the most valuable parts of this internship was getting to meet wonderful people all across Swagelok. Through networking 1:1s, Lunch and Learn's, and facility tours, I was able to gain a deeper understanding of how the business operates from manufacturing all the way to sales, and all of the departments in between that keep everything running like a well-oiled machine. Thank you, Swagelok, for an unforgettable summer. Looking forward to what's next. #AdventureAwaits

Three years, hundreds of hoodies shipped, and countless 1am calls later, my journey as a ScioVirtual Director is coming to a close. Over the past five months, I had the pleasure of co-directing ScioVirtual’s 7th edition of ScioCamp! It marked my fifth and final summer instructing the Competitive Math course, where I taught competition fundamentals and provided real-time practice - shoutout to co-instructors Gabriel, Sophia , and Aditya for helping me with the process! It is also my third and final summer helping conduct camp events and operations, though I will remain involved on ScioVirtual’s Board of Advisors (and still remain an instructor, at least for the next ScioCamp!). Some words of gratitude: First and foremost, to my fellow co-directors Om , Anahitaa , Raelle , and Tina — you are the best team of co-directors I ever could’ve asked for. Through late-night calls, last-minute leaderboard fixes, and intense email writing sessions, I am so proud of what we have accomplished for ScioVirtual. But moreover, I’m grateful to have found another home and group of friends that I could bond with over life’s circumstances, challenges, and successes. To new directors Claire , MacKhoi , Cody , Kedar , and Alice — I’m very impressed by what you all accomplished for this camp on short notice, building a new registration webpage and curating two unique challenges among other exciting developments. I’m so excited to see what’s in store at ScioCamp 2027, and I am confident you all will do amazing. Thank you for bearing with us while figuring it all out and for your dedication to making this year’s camp awesome! To former directors Sehej, Michelle , Shreyash , and Harshit — I can’t express how thankful I am to have had the opportunity to be at ScioVirtual, no less as a director, and for the guidance you all gave me and the rest of the team when we were learning how to manage camp ourselves. Last but not least, to the ScioVirtual community — all the instructors, counselors, and campers of ScioCamp — you are what makes ScioCamp and the ScioVirtual community so special! I appreciate every one of you for your role in making this possible: instructors making high quality and engaging lessons for campers, counselors for guiding kids through camp challenges, and campers for bearing with us while the leaderboard is under maintenance for days at a time. Finally, some statistics from the past three summers of ScioCamp: - Over 1100 unique students and 100 unique schools reached across all three camps - Raised $125,000+ in revenue, of which $44,000+ was donated back to local/national charities - A 90%+ increase in camp size from 2023 (299 campers at ScioCamp 2023, 570+ campers at ScioCamp 2026) - 400+ applications received for teaching positions While this is the end of my ScioVirtual directing journey, I know that when one door closes, another one opens — and I'm excited for what's to come.

My team and I just won the LinkedIn Possibilities in Tech Hackathon! This past week, I had the incredible opportunity to be flown out to LinkedIn HQ in Mountain View, CA, to compete alongside some of the brightest tech talent from across the country. After an intense few days of building, collaborating, pitching (and an impressive amount of AI prompting) our team took home first place! We created Locked[IN], a LinkedIn feature designed to help Gen Z students and individuals displaced by AI navigate the modern workforce. So many people only hear about the same few job titles; our goal was to help users uncover lesser-known career paths and provide clear, actionable steps to get there. A massive thank you to my amazing teammates, Namyanzi Edwards , Daniel Lee , and Muhammed Ali and to our mentor, Jaden Hinton . I’m also deeply grateful to Tori Goyette , Jocelyn Kuo , Pablo Najera , and everyone behind the LinkedIn Possibilities in Tech Program for organizing such an impactful event and creating this opportunity. Without all of you, this project would not have been possible. Excited to take these connections, lessons, and momentum forward! #LinkedIn #PossibilitiesInTech #Hackathon #Innovation
